description: Massacre at Glencoe, the failed Darien Scheme and the Act of Union 1707.
content_html:
Scotland After 1688

Scotland’s response to the Glorious Revolution was divided. Most Scots accepted the replacement of James VII (James II of England) with William and Mary, but Jacobite Highlanders loyal to the Stuarts mounted an immediate uprising. At the Battle of Killiecrankie (July 1689), Jacobite forces under “Bonnie Dundee” (John Graham of Claverhouse) routed a Williamite army, though Dundee was killed in the moment of victory. Without his leadership the rising collapsed, and Scotland settled — uneasily — into the new Protestant constitutional order.

The Massacre of Glencoe, 1692

The most infamous event of William’s reign in Scotland was the Massacre of Glencoe on 13 February 1692. William III had ordered all Highland clan chiefs to swear an oath of loyalty to him by 1 January 1692. Alasdair Maclain, chief of the MacDonalds of Glencoe, arrived a few days late to swear the oath. Government officials used this technicality as a pretext. A company of Campbell soldiers were billeted with the MacDonalds for two weeks, enjoying traditional Highland hospitality, before receiving orders to kill all MacDonalds under 70. Between 38 and 78 people were killed; many more died of exposure fleeing into winter snowfields.

Key Fact

Glencoe was significant not for its death toll alone, but for the violation of Highland laws of hospitality — soldiers killed their hosts. The orders were traced back to the Master of Stair (Secretary for Scotland) and arguably to William III himself. A parliamentary inquiry condemned it as “murder under trust”, though no one faced prosecution.

The Darien Scheme, 1698–1700

Scotland’s most catastrophic independent venture was the Darien Scheme, devised by William Paterson, founder of the Bank of England. A Scottish joint-stock company raised around £400,000 — estimated at a quarter of Scotland’s liquid capital — to establish a colony at Darien on the Isthmus of Panama. It aimed to control trade between the Atlantic and Pacific. William III, under pressure from English merchants who feared Scottish competition, refused to provide English navy support and warned English and Dutch colonies not to aid the Scots. The venture failed catastrophically: disease, Spanish attack and lack of supplies killed thousands of settlers. By 1700 the colony was abandoned. The financial devastation left Scotland economically desperate and its Parliament deeply resentful of England.

The Darien disaster left Scotland economically weakened and politically angry. It demonstrated that Scotland could not pursue independent trade or colonial expansion while England blocked it. At the same time, England needed Scotland’s border security, especially with France as a constant enemy. These pressures — Scottish economic need and English strategic interest — drove both parliaments toward union. Commissioners negotiated a treaty in 1706; after fierce debate and alleged bribery of Scottish MPs, it was ratified as the Act of Union in 1707.

The Act of Union, 1707

The Act of Union created the Kingdom of Great Britain on 1 May 1707. Scotland’s Parliament was abolished; Scottish MPs and peers joined Westminster. Scotland retained its own legal system, Church of Scotland, and educational institutions. Scotland gained access to English colonial trade — a crucial economic benefit after Darien. The Union was deeply unpopular with ordinary Scots: the writer Daniel Defoe, working as an English spy in Edinburgh before the vote, reported widespread hostility on the streets. Robert Burns later wrote of Scotland being “bought and sold for English gold.” Whether the Union was freely negotiated or imposed through bribery and financial necessity is still debated by Scottish historians.

Key Fact

Under the Act of Union (1707): Scotland kept its Kirk (Church of Scotland), separate legal system, and universities. It gained access to English colonial trade, financial stability, and representation at Westminster. Scotland lost its independent Parliament.

Union did not end Jacobite sentiment. In 1715, the Earl of Mar raised a Jacobite army in Scotland, nominally supporting James Francis Edward Stuart (“the Old Pretender”). “The Fifteen” was poorly led: the indecisive Battle of Sheriffmuir (November 1715) left both sides claiming partial victory. James arrived late and the rising fizzled out. Its failure demonstrated that Hanoverian rule was established enough to withstand an armed challenge, but Jacobite loyalty persisted in the Highlands until the final defeat at Culloden in 1746.
exam_tip_html: For questions on the Act of Union, make sure you can explain both causes (Darien’s economic collapse, English strategic need, Act of Settlement) and consequences (Scotland joining British colonial trade, loss of Parliament). The Massacre of Glencoe tests the theme of the Crown’s relationship with Highland Scotland — focus on why it was “murder under trust” and what the parliamentary investigation revealed about accountability.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Massacre of Glencoe (13 February 1692) killed between 38 and 78 MacDonalds; its political significance lay in the violation of Highland hospitality and the “murder under trust” verdict by a parliamentary inquiry.
  • The Darien Scheme (1698–1700) lost around a quarter of Scotland’s liquid capital and demonstrated Scotland could not pursue independent colonial trade while England blocked it — a direct push factor toward the Act of Union.
  • The Act of Union (1707) merged the English and Scottish Parliaments into a single Parliament of Great Britain; Scotland retained its Kirk, legal system and universities but gained access to English colonial trade.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Massacre of Glencoe (1692).
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Precise feature with accurate supporting detail (e.g. Campbell soldiers killed their MacDonald hosts after two weeks of hospitality, violating Highland laws of trust). Secure: Correct feature with some detail. Developing: Vague reference without specific support. Emerging: Incorrect or irrelevant response.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Darien Scheme (1698–1700).
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two precise features (e.g. aimed to establish a colony at Panama; lost approximately a quarter of Scotland's liquid capital) each with accurate detail. Secure: Two features, at least one with detail. Developing: One feature with detail, or two without. Emerging: Vague or inaccurate response.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Darien Scheme's failure helped bring about the Act of Union in 1707.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed explanation linking Darien's financial devastation to Scotland's economic weakness, England's colonial blocking, and the mutual strategic incentives for union, with precise evidence. Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence; at least one causal link explained. Developing: Some explanation with basic evidence; may be descriptive. Emerging: Simple points with limited evidence.

practice_questions.text: How significant was the Act of Union (1707) for Scotland? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument evaluating short-term gains (colonial trade, financial stability) against losses (Parliament, sovereignty), with long-term assessment (Jacobite risings, continued popular hostility) and counter-argument (economic recovery). Secure: Clear argument with evidence across more than one dimension. Developing: Some argument; may focus on only one aspect. Emerging: Simple points with limited evidence.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the Massacre of Glencoe (1692) damaged William III's reputation in Scotland.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed explanation showing the orders traced back to William or his government, the violation of Highland hospitality ('murder under trust'), and the parliamentary condemnation without prosecution. Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence. Developing: Basic reason with limited evidence. Emerging: Vague or incorrect response.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Act of Union (1707).
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two precise features (e.g. abolition of the Scottish Parliament; Scotland gained access to English colonial trade) each with accurate detail. Secure: Two features, at least one with detail. Developing: One feature with detail, or two without. Emerging: Vague or inaccurate response.

glossary_terms.definition: The killing of between 38 and 78 members of the MacDonald clan at Glencoe on 13 February 1692, carried out by Campbell troops acting on government orders.
Scotland's failed attempt 1698–1700 to establish a trading colony on the Darien peninsula (modern Panama), which resulted in the loss of around a quarter of Scotland's liquid capital.
The 1707 treaty that merged the Kingdom of England and the Kingdom of Scotland into a single Kingdom of Great Britain, with one Parliament at Westminster.
